report:
## Conclusion

Yes—modest evidence supports honey as a helpful, low-risk remedy for acute cough in children **over age 1**. The Cochrane systematic review (Oduwole 2018, updated 2023) and a more recent systematic review found low- to moderate-quality evidence that honey reduces cough symptom scores and improves children's sleep more than no treatment, placebo, or diphenhydramine, and works about as well as dextromethorphan (a common OTC cough suppressant) (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/). An earlier randomized trial published in JAMA Pediatrics likewise found that a single nighttime dose of buckwheat honey outperformed both dextromethorphan and no treatment for nocturnal cough and sleep disruption in children with upper respiratory infections (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/571638).

Important caveats: the underlying trials are few, small, short-duration (often just one night), and heterogeneous, so evidence quality is rated low-to-moderate, and effects may partly reflect the natural resolution of colds rather than a specific pharmacologic action of honey. Honey is not a cure for the underlying infection and does not shorten illness duration—it primarily eases symptom severity.

**Safety limit:** Honey must never be given to infants under 12 months old, because of the risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores it may contain; it is considered safe only after age 1 (https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/honey-botulism.html).

**Bottom line:** For children over 1 year with a common cold–related cough, honey (e.g., a teaspoon before bedtime) is a reasonable, inexpensive, safe alternative to OTC cough medicines and may modestly relieve cough symptoms and improve sleep, though better-designed trials are still needed.
